title: The first major cast-iron bridge was held together with woodworking joints

cover.alt: The Iron Bridge, a single dark-red cast-iron arch with lacy ribs and rings, crossing the wooded River Severn gorge.

body: **The Iron Bridge** over the River Severn in Shropshire, England, opened in 1781 as the first major bridge in the world made of cast iron. Yet it follows a carpenters' design of the kind used for wooden structures. Thomas Gregory, a foreman at Abraham Darby III's foundry, drew the detailed parts, and the result was iron jointed like timber, with **mortise and tenon joints and dovetails**. Its almost 1,700 pieces were each cast to fit their neighbours rather than to standard sizes, so parts that look identical can differ by several centimetres. The bridge's success helped make cast iron a common building material.

slides.alt: A curly red cast-iron panel in the bridge's railings reading 'Erected in 1779', with the river and village of Ironbridge behind.
slides.caption: The railings still carry the date. The arch first spanned the river in July 1779, and the bridge opened to traffic on 1 January 1781.
slides.credit: The Ironbridge Gorge Museum · CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.question: How many tonnes of iron went into the bridge?
slides.explanation: 384.6 tonnes, or exactly 378 long tons 10 hundredweight, spread across almost 1,700 separately cast pieces.

slides.heading: Planned cost versus what it really cost
slides.note: Contemporary records suggest up to £6,000. Darby, already in debt, agreed to cover the excess.

slides.heading: Built on moving ground
slides.text: The gorge's banks are unstable and prone to landslides. Cracks appeared within a few years of opening, and repairs went on for two centuries. In 1972 to 1975 engineers put a reinforced-concrete inverted arch under the river to brace the foundations.

slides.heading: A clue from a painting
slides.text: In 1997 a watercolour by Elias Martin turned up in a Stockholm museum, showing the bridge under construction in 1779. In 2001 researchers for the BBC's Timewatch built a half-size replica of the main section using the method it shows.

slides.clue: A woodworking joint with interlocking, flared parts, used with mortise and tenons to fit the bridge's iron.
slides.detail: Foundry foreman Thomas Gregory drew the parts using carpentry joints like this one.
